rubric.why: Metabolism is defined as the sum of the chemical reactions occurring in an organism.
rubric.description: Defines metabolism as the sum of chemical reactions in the body or organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition that identifies the reactions as occurring in the organism.

rubric.why: Anabolism and catabolism are the two types of metabolism.
rubric.description: Names both types of metabolism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark only when both types are named.

modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions taking place in the body of an organism.
The two types of metabolism are anabolism and catabolism.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme’s active site helps it act on a specific substrate.

rubric.why: The lock-and-key model explains enzyme specificity through the matching shapes of the active site and substrate.
rubric.description: Explains that only a substrate with a matching shape fits the enzyme’s active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate fits or matches the active site specifically.

rubric.why: The enzyme-substrate complex leads to product formation, while the enzyme remains available for reuse.
rubric.description: States that products form and the enzyme is unchanged or reusable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the product-formation step and the enzyme remaining unchanged or reusable.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, an enzyme has an active site with a specific shape that matches its substrate, just as a lock matches its key.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; the reaction produces products, which leave while the enzyme remains unchanged and can be reused.

rubric.why: Cohesion is attraction between molecules of the same substance.
rubric.description: Defines cohesion as attraction between molecules of the same substance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the attraction as occurring between like molecules.

rubric.why: Adhesion is attraction between molecules of different substances.
rubric.description: Defines adhesion as attraction between molecules of different substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the attraction as occurring between unlike substances.

modelAnswer: Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance, such as water molecules attracting one another.
Adhesion is the attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water molecules attracting the walls of a xylem vessel.

items.followUp: Differentiate between an ecosystem and a population.

rubric.why: A population consists of members of one species living in a particular area at the same time.
rubric.description: Explains population level of organization.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for identifying members as belonging to the same species and 1 for identifying that they live in the same area at the same time.

rubric.why: A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
rubric.description: Explains community level of organization.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for describing different populations or species and 1 for stating that they live or interact in the same area.

modelAnswer: Population level: A population consists of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time; for example, all the frogs in a pond.
Community level: A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area; for example, the plants, animals and microorganisms in a pond.

items.followUp: Explain how active transport enables root hair cells to absorb mineral ions from the soil.

rubric.why: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient.
rubric.description: States the direction of movement against the concentration gradient.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing movement from lower to higher concentration or against the gradient.

rubric.why: Active transport requires energy, commonly supplied by ATP from respiration.
rubric.description: Identifies the energy requirement and its source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming energy and, preferably, ATP or respiration.

rubric.why: Membrane transport proteins help move substances across the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Describes the role of carrier or transport proteins in the membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying membrane proteins as involved in transport.

rubric.why: Root hair cells use active transport to take up mineral ions from the soil, even when the soil concentration is lower.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of active transport in plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mineral-ion uptake by root hair cells from soil.

rubric.why: Active transport moves particular substances across membranes and is important in cellular absorption and uptake.
rubric.description: Adds a relevant feature or further example of active transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that transport is selective or naming a valid example such as glucose or amino-acid absorption.

modelAnswer: Active transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, from a lower concentration to a higher concentration.
It requires energy, usually supplied as ATP during respiration.
Carrier or transport proteins in the cell membrane assist in moving the substances.
For example, root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, even when their concentration is lower in the soil than in the cells.
Active transport is selective and also helps cells absorb substances such as glucose and amino acids.

items.followUp: Compare the cell structure and nutrition of Monera, Protista, and Fungi.

rubric.why: Monera are prokaryotic, while Protista are eukaryotic; members of both kingdoms are generally unicellular.
rubric.description: Gives distinguishing characteristics of Monera and Protista.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for correctly identifying Monera as prokaryotic and Protista as eukaryotic, with their usual unicellular organization.

rubric.why: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that generally absorb nutrients, whereas plants are eukaryotic autotrophs that photosynthesize.
rubric.description: Gives distinguishing characteristics of Fungi and Plantae.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for correctly describing fungi and plants, including their contrasting modes of nutrition.

rubric.why: Animals are multicellular eukaryotic heterotrophs and their cells lack cell walls.
rubric.description: States characteristic features of Animalia.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct characteristic set for animals.

modelAnswer: Monera: Organisms are unicellular and prokaryotic; they lack a membrane-bound nucleus. They may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
Protista: Organisms are eukaryotic and mostly unicellular; some are autotrophic and others heterotrophic.
Fungi: Organisms are eukaryotic and mostly multicellular, with cell walls; they are heterotrophic and absorb nutrients from their surroundings.
Plantae: Organisms are multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls; they are mainly autotrophic and make food by photosynthesis.
Animalia: Organisms are multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; they are heterotrophic and usually capable of movement.

items.followUp: Describe how the liver helps regulate blood glucose and remove waste products.

rubric.why: The liver produces bile, which helps in the digestion of fats by emulsifying them.
rubric.description: States that the liver produces bile and gives its role in fat digestion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for bile production and its digestive role.

rubric.why: The liver converts excess glucose to glycogen and helps regulate blood glucose.
rubric.description: Describes glucose regulation through glycogen storage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that excess glucose is stored as glycogen.

rubric.why: The liver deaminates excess amino acids and converts the resulting ammonia into urea.
rubric.description: Describes the liver’s role in urea formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking deamination or ammonia with urea production.

rubric.why: The liver detoxifies harmful substances and also performs storage functions such as storing vitamins.
rubric.description: Gives another valid liver function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct additional function, such as detoxification or storage of vitamins.

modelAnswer: The liver produces bile, which emulsifies fats and helps their digestion.
It converts excess glucose in the blood into glycogen for storage and helps regulate blood glucose levels.
It deaminates excess amino acids and converts the resulting ammonia into urea.
It detoxifies harmful substances, including some drugs and poisons, and stores vitamins and minerals.

items.followUp: Trace the path of blood through the human heart, naming the chambers and valves.

rubric.why: The human heart is a muscular organ with two atria and two ventricles.
rubric.description: Identifies the four chambers of the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming or correctly describing the two atria and two ventricles.

rubric.why: The septum separates the right and left sides, and valves prevent backflow of blood.
rubric.description: Describes the septum or heart valves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct statement about the septum and/or valves.

rubric.why: Blood returns from the body to the right side and is pumped to the lungs; oxygenated blood returns to the left side and is pumped to the body.
rubric.description: Gives the correct route of blood through the heart and major vessels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct route including chambers and major vessels.

rubric.why: A clear, correctly oriented, labelled diagram should show the chambers, septum, valves and major vessels.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled diagram of the heart.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for a clear diagram: 1 for the four correctly positioned chambers and septum, and 1 for correctly labelling major vessels and showing the direction of blood flow.

modelAnswer: The heart is a hollow, muscular organ enclosed by a protective covering; it has four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.
The septum separates the right and left sides of the heart; valves between the chambers and at the exits of the ventricles prevent backflow.
The venae cavae bring deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium; it passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and leaves through the pulmonary artery for the lungs.
Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium; it passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve to the left ventricle and leaves through the aorta for the body.
Diagram construction: Draw a heart outline 6 cm high and 5 cm wide, with the apex pointing downwards; divide it vertically into right and left sides with a septum.
In the upper half, draw and label two chambers, each about 2 cm wide: right atrium on the viewer’s left and left atrium on the viewer’s right.
In the lower half, draw and label two chambers, each about 2.5 cm wide: right ventricle on the viewer’s left and left ventricle on the viewer’s right; draw the left ventricle wall thicker.
Draw and label the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, and the bicuspid valve between the left atrium and left ventricle.

Draw the venae cavae entering the right atrium, the pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle, the pulmonary veins entering the left atrium and the aorta leaving the left ventricle; add arrows to show the direction of blood flow.
